title: Samson's Wedding and the Riddle of the Lion
summary: Samson demands a Philistine wife from Timnah, over his parents' objections. On the way he kills a lion with his bare hands and later eats honey from its carcass, then uses the event for a riddle at his wedding feast. The Philistine guests force his bride to extract the answer, and in fury Samson kills thirty men of Ashkelon to pay his wager, returning home while his wife is given to another man.
story: Chapter 13 announced a boy set apart for God who would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. Chapter 14 shows the grown man, and the contrast is immediate. Samson is driven by what is pleasing to his eyes, ignores his parents, handles a carcass, and hosts a drinking feast, and the only deliverance in view is personal revenge. Yet the narrator inserts a note in 14:4 that his parents did not know this was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines. The chapter sets the pattern of the whole Samson story: a man pursuing his own desires and grudges, and a God who uses even those to weaken Israel's oppressors.
historical:
Timnah lay in the Sorek Valley, a few miles west of Zorah and Eshtaol, on the border between Israelite and Philistine territory. It is usually identified with Tel Batash, where excavations have found remains from Philistine and Israelite periods. The Sorek Valley was one of the natural routes from the coastal plain into the hill country, and its towns were contested. That Samson can travel freely to Timnah and marry into a Philistine family shows how the two peoples lived side by side, with the Philistines ruling but not always at war.

The note that the Philistines were ruling over Israel (14:4) confirms the setting of 13:1. Ashkelon, where Samson goes to take the thirty garments, was one of the five Philistine cities, on the Mediterranean coast more than twenty miles from Timnah. The choice of a distant city may have been meant to avoid immediate reprisal at Timnah, but the text doesn't say.
cultural:
Marriage was arranged by families, and Samson's demand that his parents get the woman for him reflects that custom, even as his refusal of their advice breaks it. Israel's law forbade marriage with the peoples of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:3-4), and the Philistines, uncircumcised and worshipers of other gods, fell within the spirit of that warning, which is why his parents object. Some interpreters think the marriage described here is one in which the wife remained in her father's house and the husband visited, a form known in the ancient Near East; the scene in 15:1 fits that possibility.

Wedding feasts lasted seven days (compare Jacob's wedding in Genesis 29:27). The word used here for feast (mishteh) comes from the verb to drink, which suggests a drinking party and raises the question of Samson's Nazirite abstinence from wine, though the text doesn't say whether he drank. The thirty companions were customary attendants for a bridegroom, but here they also look like a guard. Riddles and wagers were a common entertainment. Linen garments and changes of clothes were valuable goods, and thirty of each was a large stake.
literary: The chapter is full of word play and repetition. What is right in Samson's eyes (14:3, 14:7) anticipates the book's closing refrain that everyone did what was right in his own eyes. The riddle, “Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet” (14:14), is unanswerable without private knowledge. The Philistines' reply, “What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?” (14:18), is itself shaped like a riddle, and some scholars suggest it may have been a known riddle whose usual answer was love. Samson's retort about plowing with his heifer is a crude and bitter image. The Spirit of the LORD rushes upon him twice, with the same Hebrew verb (14:6, 14:19), framing the chapter's violence. Repeated secrets also structure the story: Samson doesn't tell his parents about the lion or the honey, and the secret he keeps from his wife becomes the one she betrays.

outline.t: Samson demands a Philistine wife from Timnah
The lion torn apart and the honey from its carcass
The wedding feast and the riddle
The bride pressured, and the riddle revealed
Thirty men killed at Ashkelon; the bride given away

doctrines.note: God works through Samson's self-centered choices to confront the Philistines (14:4). This is not approval of Samson's desires but a claim that God can direct even flawed human choices toward his purposes.

The Spirit of the LORD rushes upon Samson with physical power. In Judges the Spirit equips people for particular acts of deliverance, and the gift does not guarantee the recipient's holiness or wisdom.

Samson follows what pleases his eyes, dishonors his parents' counsel, and ignores his Nazirite vow. His strength is real, but his character is undisciplined, and the chapter traces the harm that follows.

words.note: Chidah, a riddle or enigmatic saying, used eight times in this chapter. The word can also mean a hard question (as when the queen of Sheba tests Solomon in 1 Kings 10:1) or a parable. Here it is a game with high stakes, and it exposes the distrust between Samson and his Philistine hosts.

Tsalach, to rush or come powerfully, describing the Spirit's action in 14:6 and 14:19. The same verb is used of the Spirit coming upon Saul and David in 1 Samuel. It suggests a sudden, overpowering force that equips a person for an immediate task.

To'anah, an occasion or opportunity, found only here in the Hebrew Bible. The narrator says the LORD was seeking an occasion against the Philistines (14:4). The word frames the entire Samson story: God is not caught off guard by Samson's choices but uses them for his purpose.

Patah, to entice or persuade, sometimes to deceive. The Philistines demand that Samson's wife entice him (14:15), and the same verb is used when the Philistine lords ask Delilah to entice him in 16:5. The repetition ties the two betrayals together.

christ: The link to Christ in this chapter is mainly by contrast. Samson is a deliverer whose strength comes from the Spirit, but he uses it for personal vengeance and pursues what pleases his eyes. Jesus, on whom the Spirit descended at his baptism (Luke 3:22), used that power to heal, to serve, and finally to lay down his life. Samson took a bride from among his enemies, and the relationship ended in betrayal and death. The New Testament speaks of Christ loving his people while they were still enemies (Romans 5:10) and giving himself for his bride, the church (Ephesians 5:25). The riddle of the lion, strength yielding sweetness, has sometimes been read by Christian preachers as a picture of the gospel, but that is a devotional application, not the meaning of the text.

hard.q: How can Samson's choices be from the LORD if they break God's law and are driven by selfish desire?
hard.a: The narrator's comment in 14:4 is carefully worded. It doesn't say God approved Samson's desire for a Philistine wife, only that God was seeking an occasion against the Philistines through it. Scripture regularly affirms that God works through human sin without causing or excusing it: Joseph tells his brothers that they meant evil but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20), and the crucifixion is described as both the wicked act of men and part of God's plan (Acts 2:23). Christian theologians have described this as God's providence governing all things while human beings remain responsible for their choices. Some interpreters stress that 14:4 is about God's purpose, not Samson's motives, and that Samson is fully accountable. Others think the verse suggests God stirred Samson's attraction for his own ends. The chapter does not settle the philosophy; it simply insists that neither Samson's recklessness nor Philistine power is outside God's control.

questions: Samson chose what was right in his own eyes. How do desire and sight shape your decisions, and what helps you see differently?
Samson's parents did not understand what God was doing. How do you hold together trust in God's purposes and honest disapproval of wrong choices?
Samson's strength came from the Spirit, but his character was undisciplined. Why do you think Scripture shows gifted leaders with such serious flaws?
